title: Do people prefer traditional architecture? - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Roughly twenty properly sampled visual preference surveys since the 1990s show 60-92 percent of the public prefers traditional architecture over modernist designs, with the preference holding across age, gender, politics, race, income and nationality; AI image editing has recently collapsed the cost of producing tightly controlled image pairs, creating a 'golden age' of such surveying. The author's closing puzzle is a stated-versus-revealed preference gap: over 99 percent of architects practice modernist styles and Britain has commissioned almost no public building in a traditional style since the 1950s, even in stylistically neutral planning regimes.

themes.theme: The headline finding: a 70-90 percent traditionalist supermajority

insights.claim: Across every properly sampled visual preference survey on architectural style run since the 1990s, more than 60 percent of respondents have favored traditional architecture, with many studies showing over 85 percent support.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A consistent 60-90 percent consumer preference that the supply side ignores is the classic setup for an underserved market; watch housebuilders and developers who can price traditional facades at a premium.
insights.quote: In every survey conducted, over 60 percent of the respondents have favored traditional architecture, with many revealing over 85 percent support.
insights.locator: In every survey conducted, over 60 percent

insights.claim: The author's provisional bottom line is that 70 to 90 percent of the population has a clear preference for traditional architecture, with every demographic group — men and women, old and young, rich and poor — favoring traditional design, and demographic tilts being only slight.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Because the preference is demographically flat, it can't be dismissed as a niche or aging-cohort taste — it will not fade as boomers exit the market.
insights.quote: For now, the provisional conclusion is that 70 to 90 percent of the population has a clear preference for traditional architecture.
insights.locator: For now, the provisional conclusion

insights.claim: The preference for traditional design extends beyond housing to hospitals, commercial buildings and civic buildings, meaning it is not confined to the one segment (private housing) where the market already supplies it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The gap between preference and supply is widest in institutional and commercial property, where procurement is professionalized — the likeliest place for a policy or reputational shock.
insights.quote: This holds not only for houses but also for hospitals and commercial and civic buildings.
insights.locator: This holds not only for houses

insights.claim: In a 1998 British Market Research Bureau survey for the Popular Housing Forum, 94 percent of potential newbuild buyers said they would prefer to live in one of the more traditional options and 92 percent of other respondents preferred a traditional option to be built near them.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Near-unanimous buyer preference in the one segment that is genuinely market-driven explains why UK volume housebuilders already build pastiche traditional — and why the pattern breaks in non-market segments.
insights.quote: 94 percent of potential newbuild buyers said they would prefer to live in one of the more traditional options
insights.locator: The first properly sampled visual preference survey followed in 1998

themes.theme: Preference is demographically flat — including politically

insights.claim: In the 2020 National Civic Art Society survey of US federal and courthouse buildings, traditional designs won by an average of 72 percent across seven controlled image pairs, with essentially no partisan split: 70 percent of Democrats and 73 percent of Republicans preferred traditional.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A design-standards mandate for federal buildings is one of the rare policy levers with genuine cross-party polling cover — low political cost, so it can move faster than most expect.
insights.quote: There was almost no correlation with political affiliation, with 70 percent of Democrats and 73 percent of Republicans preferring the traditional designs.
insights.locator: As in other studies, most striking is how little

insights.claim: In the same US survey, 75 percent of white Americans, 65 percent of Hispanic Americans and 62 percent of black Americans preferred traditional designs, with no significant correlation to income or education and age only a weak predictor (77 percent of over-65s versus 68 percent of 18-34s).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Kills the 'elite versus populist' and 'old versus young' framings of the architecture debate — the only real cleavage left is professional versus lay.
insights.locator: 75 percent of white Americans preferred traditional architecture

insights.claim: The demographic tilts that do exist are weak and not always in the expected direction: in the HS2 viaduct survey, Labour voters were slightly more pro-traditional than Conservatives (72 versus 69 percent) and younger respondents more pro-traditional than older ones (70 versus 64 percent).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that traditionalism is a right-coded or nostalgic preference; the political economy of design standards is less predictable than the culture-war framing implies.
insights.quote: Anomalously, the survey also found that Labour voters were slightly more pro-traditional than Conservatives (72 against 69 percent) and younger people more than older people
insights.locator: These results varied only modestly along demographic lines

insights.claim: Even in the youngest cohort most open to modernism, the traditional option still wins decisively: 18-24 year olds preferred the classical Bath stadium design by 61 to 39 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The generational-replacement argument for modernism has no empirical support — a preference this stable across cohorts is a durable demand signal, not a fashion cycle.
insights.locator: Older people were, as in most studies, more traditional

themes.theme: AI as the enabling technology for controlled preference research

insights.claim: Artificial intelligence has sharply cut the time and cost of generating matched architectural images, making reliable large-scale visual preference surveys feasible for the first time and driving what the author calls a golden age of the method since roughly 2020.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A cheap AI capability is unlocking a whole class of evidence that was previously cost-prohibited — a template for where else generative imaging turns qualitative debates into settled empirical ones.
insights.quote: In the past few years, artificial intelligence has greatly reduced the time and costs of producing comparable images, making reliable large-scale visual preference surveys far more feasible.
insights.locator: In the past few years, artificial intelligence

insights.claim: The Aesthetic City's 2025 Dutch survey used AI to generate the traditional counterfactual from a photograph of an actual modernist building in all but one of eight image pairs, holding context, weather and massing constant — a methodology that removes the standard confounders critics used to dismiss earlier studies.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The photograph-plus-AI-counterfactual pair is now the reference method; expect every future architecture consultation fight to be argued with these images.
insights.quote: In all but one image pair, they used a photograph of a modernist building and then used AI to create the traditional alternative.
insights.locator: The Dutch study is notable for showing how useful artificial intelligence is

insights.claim: Dutch respondents in the 2025 Aesthetic City survey preferred traditional buildings in a range of 67 to 92 percent across eight image pairs, averaging 82 percent — higher than comparable British or American results.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Continental results running above Anglo ones suggests the finding is not an artifact of British royal-patronage politics; the effect travels.
insights.locator: Continental Europeans appear to prefer traditional architecture

insights.claim: David Halpern's 1987 Cambridge study found that architecture students and non-architecture students agreed closely on which faces were attractive but held wildly divergent, often directly opposite, views on buildings — evidence that architectural training, not general aesthetic sense, is what separates professional from public taste.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The face-rating control is the key analytical move: it isolates professional socialization as the cause, which means the supply-side blockage sits in architecture schools, not in some innate elite sensibility.
insights.quote: Students on different programs had similar views on which faces were the most attractive. But when it came to buildings, architecture students held wildly different views from those in other disciplines.
insights.locator: Halpern showed volunteer students photographs of twelve people and twelve buildings

insights.claim: The Halpern expert-lay divergence has been replicated in Canada in 2001, Britain in 2015 and Chile in 2019, making it one of the more robust cross-national findings in the literature.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Replication across three continents and thirty years means the professional-public gap is structural, not a local quirk — it will not self-correct.
insights.locator: studies have since been run in Canada in 2001

insights.claim: Luis Balula's 2008-2009 survey in Evora, Portugal found experts and non-experts converged in rating older buildings highly but inverted on modern designs — non-experts liked a pastiche Mediterranean housing group that experts disliked, and experts rated positively a modernist apartment block that non-experts rated negatively.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Agreement on heritage but inversion on new build localizes the conflict precisely to new construction — the only place where it costs money.
insights.locator: Portuguese researcher Luis Balula carried out a visual preference survey

insights.claim: The Commission for Architecture and the Built Environment's 2005 report expressed regret that modern styles' advantages in light and large windows 'does not seem to have been understood by home buyers', which the author reads as evidence that professionals interpret contrary public preference as public failure to understand rather than as a signal.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
entities: Commission for Architecture and the Built Environment
insights.so_what: When even the public body commissioning the research treats the result as a comprehension problem, the feedback loop from consumer preference to supply is broken by design.
insights.quote: The Modern Movement’s concern for light and sun and large windows should give a modern style a clear advantage over more traditional designs, but this advantage does not seem to have been understood by home buyers
insights.locator: Two visual preference surveys were commissioned in 2002 and 2005

insights.claim: Prize-winning modernist buildings do not close the gap: in ADAM Architecture's 2009 survey, two award-winning modernist commercial buildings drew only 23 percent support against 77 percent for two traditional designs, despite matched perspectives and lighting.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the 'they only tested bad modernism' defense — professional acclaim and public appeal are close to inversely related.
insights.quote: Both of the modernist buildings had won prizes, suggesting that they were especially well-designed examples. Even so, only 23 percent of respondents preferred them
insights.locator: One of the best early visual preference surveys was commissioned

insights.claim: Even the world's most prestigious practices lose these head-to-heads: 71 percent of over 2,000 British adults preferred Create Streets' Gothic counterproposal for a new Christ's College Cambridge library to the actual 2025 proposal by Grafton Architects, which got 21 percent.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Star-architect brand equity carries no weight with the public, which weakens the reputational justification institutions use for premium design fees.
insights.locator: In 2025, Christ's College Cambridge announced plans

themes.theme: Live UK development fights as natural experiments

insights.claim: Create Streets' survey of 3,130 British adults on the Marks and Spencer Oxford Street site produced its strongest result ever: 79 percent backed a Francis Terry scheme retaining and extending the existing 1920s facade at the same floor area, against 17 percent for M&S's demolition-and-modern-rebuild plan.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Retrofit-plus-facade-retention schemes carry overwhelming public support at equal floor area, which strengthens objectors' hand in high-profile demolition consents and raises planning risk for demolition-led retail and office redevelopment.
insights.locator: The British retailer Marks and Spencer is planning to demolish

insights.claim: Londoners were only marginally more favorable to Marks and Spencer's modern proposal than the national average and still backed the traditional Terry scheme 72 to 26 percent, undercutting the idea that urban, design-literate populations are the constituency for modernism.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Developers cannot appeal to a sophisticated local audience to justify contested schemes — the local electorate polls the same as everyone else.
insights.locator: Londoners were a little more likely to favor

insights.claim: The public's preference for traditional treatment extends to infrastructure, not just buildings: a Create Streets survey found 69 percent preferred a red-brick-clad HS2 viaduct emulating nineteenth-century railway viaducts against 28 percent for HS2's planned concrete design, with only building treatment varying between images.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cladding and treatment choices on megaprojects are a cheap lever for public consent; infrastructure sponsors facing local opposition may be leaving easy goodwill on the table.
insights.locator: The same trend shows up in infrastructure

insights.claim: In the Shoreditch Works poll, 76 to 78 percent of respondents preferred proposed traditionally-styled office blocks drawing on Victorian commercial and Art Deco precedent over existing postwar warehouses, even though the new buildings were drastically taller — a test deliberately loaded against the traditional option by the usual assumption that the public dislikes high-rise.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Suggests style can buy density: developers may be able to trade traditional facade treatment for additional height in contested urban schemes, a directly monetizable finding.
insights.quote: The standard view is that the public dislikes high-rise development, meaning that this study could be seen as ‘biased against’ traditional architecture. But in each case, between 76 and 78 percent of respondents preferred the proposed scheme
insights.locator: Most of the studies we have looked at aim to control

insights.claim: Britain's unusually active visual preference survey industry is partly a product of the King's championship of traditional urbanism, which has kept architectural debate politically live there in a way it is not elsewhere.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains why the UK is the leading indicator for design-code policy shifts — watch Britain first for regulatory changes that later travel.
insights.locator: Many are British, partly because the King's championship

themes.theme: Caveats, sponsor bias and the thin evidence base

insights.claim: Perhaps only three dozen fully controlled image pairs have ever been polled, and the high-quality studies exist only in Britain, the Netherlands and the United States, so the author expects the evidence base to triple or quadruple within a decade before firm conclusions can be drawn.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Anyone building policy or a product thesis on this finding is doing so on ~36 data points — the next decade of surveys is the real catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: perhaps only three dozen fully controlled image pairs have ever been polled on
insights.locator: Visual preference surveying on architectural style is still in its infancy

insights.claim: The author concedes the strongest objection to the literature: most visual preference surveys have been commissioned by organizations sympathetic to traditional architecture, with only a handful of counterexamples like the early CABE studies, raising the suspicion of loaded image selection.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sponsor bias is the live attack line against this evidence; the fact that the sceptic-commissioned CABE studies reached the same conclusion is the strongest available rebuttal.
insights.quote: The suspicion of a loaded choice of images is heightened by the fact that most visual preference surveys have been commissioned by organizations sympathetic to traditional architecture
insights.locator: Sceptics often argue that when the public prefers

insights.claim: The single strongest defense of the finding is not any one study's quality but uniformity of sign: every image pair surveyed so far has generated the same result, with zero counterexamples across roughly twenty properly sampled surveys in six countries.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Unanimity of direction across independent sponsors and countries is harder to fake than any single effect size — the result to watch is the first genuine counterexample.
insights.quote: Nevertheless, it is striking that every image pair surveyed so far has generated the same result.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, it is striking that every image pair

insights.claim: The 1979 Metuchen, New Jersey survey run by the Rutgers University Urban Design Studio established that responses to built environments are predictable and shared rather than purely matters of individual taste, and the town later wrote a design code on the basis of its results.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Precedent that preference surveys translate directly into binding local design codes — the mechanism by which this research becomes a development constraint.
insights.quote: The Metuchen survey was the first to show that people tend to have predictable, shared responses to different built environments, responses that are not purely a matter of individual taste.
insights.locator: The birth of visual preference surveying

insights.claim: Almost every architecture school in the world teaches exclusively broadly modernist styles and probably more than 99 percent of architects practice exclusively in them, producing a supply monoculture in the face of a 70-90 percent contrary demand signal.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A near-total supply monoculture against overwhelming stated demand is either a massive latent market opportunity for traditionalist practices or evidence that the stated preference does not convert to willingness to pay — the resolution is the whole investment question.
insights.quote: Almost every architectural school in the world exclusively teaches broadly modernist styles, and probably more than 99 percent of architects practice exclusively in them.
insights.locator: If this is true, a greater puzzle comes into view

insights.claim: Britain has seen hardly a single public commission in a traditional style since the 1950s and only a trickle of commercial and institutional ones, making traditional styles virtually extinct for seven decades outside the private housing market.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Private housing being the sole surviving traditionalist segment is the tell: where consumers pay directly, traditional wins; where procurement is intermediated, it does not.
insights.quote: Except in the market for private housing, traditional styles have been virtually extinct for seven decades.
insights.locator: In Britain, there has been hardly a single public commission

insights.claim: The author rules out planning regulation as the full explanation, noting the anti-traditional trend persists in jurisdictions whose development control systems are stylistically neutral, and frames the residual as a mysterious divergence between stated and revealed preferences that the article deliberately leaves unresolved.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: If deregulation alone won't shift built output, the binding constraint sits in the architectural profession and client procurement culture — a much slower thing to arbitrage than a rule change.
insights.quote: Although in some cases this can be explained by anti-traditional planning rules, the broad trend is still evident in jurisdictions whose development control systems are stylistically neutral.
insights.locator: Although in some cases this can be explained

insights.claim: Contemporaries on both sides of the modernist debate agreed from the outset that it lacked public support, with John Summerson in 1940 saying the public 'can't understand it, never will, and hates it like poison' and the anti-modernist critic Wolf von Eckardt in 1977 declaring it 'was never popular' — meaning the new survey evidence confirms an eighty-year-old consensus rather than discovering something new.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Sustained unpopularity that was known and openly acknowledged for eighty years without changing practice is the clearest evidence that public preference is not an input into this industry at all.
insights.quote: can’t understand it, never will, and hates it like poison
insights.locator: Throughout its history, both supporters and detractors
